security.meta.title: Security & Privacy - encrypt.click
security.meta.description: How encrypt.click handles data: browser-side crypto, encrypted chat and transfers, what third parties see, and what we do not collect.
security.subtitle: A plain-language summary of how encrypt.click is designed to handle your data. For information only - not legal advice.
security.noAccounts.title: No accounts, no logins
security.noAccounts.text: encrypt.click has no user accounts, logins, or profiles. You do not need to register or provide personal information to use the tools.
security.clientSide.title: Browser-side tools
security.clientSide.p1: Developer and privacy tools, including hashing, key generation, encoding, and other local utilities, run in your browser using Web Crypto and other browser APIs. Their inputs are not uploaded to encrypt.click for processing.
security.clientSide.p2: When a tool requests public data at your direction, such as drand randomness for Time Capsule through our same-origin proxy, the request does not include your plaintext secrets or passwords.
security.shortening.title: Link shortening
security.shortening.p1: After encryption, your browser sends the share link to /api/shorten on encrypt.click, which shortens it with our own service at l.encrypt.click. No third-party shorteners are used. If shortening fails, you get the full link instead.
security.shortening.p2: The short link stores the full link including the encrypted payload, but never the password. Anyone with the short link still needs the password, so use the generated passphrase or another strong password.
security.shortening.p3: The full link keeps the payload in the URL fragment, which never leaves your browser. Share it instead of the short link if you don't want the encrypted payload stored on l.encrypt.click.
security.cookies.title: Cookies and browser storage
security.cookies.p1: The site sets one functional cookie, ec-lang, only after you pick a language in the menu. It holds the two-letter language code, nothing else, for one year, and is not used for tracking. The first visit without it is served in your browser language. Your browser may use localStorage for the theme and, when local chat history is enabled, encrypted message envelopes on your device. Session storage may briefly hold a room password while you join.
security.cookies.p2: Cloudflare (hosting) may set cookies for security and abuse prevention depending on traffic and browser settings, under Cloudflare's own policies.
security.network.title: Network and transport security
security.network.li1: All traffic is served over HTTPS with modern TLS.
security.network.li2: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) is enabled with includeSubDomains and preload.
security.network.li3: Content Security Policy (CSP) restricts scripts, styles, fonts, and connections; inline script hashes are used instead of broad unsafe-inline for scripts.
security.network.li4: Framing is disabled via frame-ancestors 'none' and X-Frame-Options: DENY.
security.thirdParty.title: Third-party infrastructure
security.thirdParty.p1: The site runs on Cloudflare Workers. Real-time chat and the whiteboard are relayed by Durable Objects in the same Worker (PartyServer). Calls may be relayed through Cloudflare TURN or another configured TURN provider. Temporary ciphertext hosts, including Send-compatible instances, may receive encrypted blobs when first-party upload is unavailable.
security.thirdParty.p2: encrypt.click does not maintain a database of your tool inputs. API abuse controls use a salted hash of the IP address held in memory for about 60 seconds. Cloudflare may also apply bot detection or challenges under its own policies.
security.disclosure.title: Responsible disclosure
security.disclosure.text: If you believe you found a security or privacy issue in encrypt.click, email mail@encrypt.click. Include enough detail to reproduce the issue and avoid testing that could impact other users.
security.nonLegal.title: Non-legal summary
security.nonLegal.text: This page is a human-readable summary of how encrypt.click is designed to handle data. It is not a contract or a complete set of legal terms. Perfect security cannot be guaranteed; you use the tools at your own risk.

tools.help.title: Quick guide
tools.base64.meta.title: Base64 Encoder & Decoder - encrypt.click
tools.base64.meta.description: Encode and decode Base64 text locally in your browser. Handy for data transport - not encryption.
tools.bcrypt.meta.title: Bcrypt Hash Generator - encrypt.click
tools.bcrypt.meta.description: Generate and verify bcrypt password hashes locally in your browser.
tools.jwt.meta.title: JWT Debugger - encrypt.click
tools.jwt.meta.description: Decode JWT headers and claims locally. Nothing is sent to a server.
tools.timeCapsule.meta.title: Time Capsule - Timelock Encryption - encrypt.click
tools.timeCapsule.meta.description: Lock a message until a future time using drand timelock encryption. Encryption stays in your browser.
tools.aesWords.help.what: Turns your text into an AES-256 encrypted payload written as ordinary English words, so it's easy to copy or read aloud.
tools.aesWords.help.safe: Encryption and decryption run in your browser. The password never leaves your device; without it the word list is just noise.
tools.aesWords.help.watchOut: Anyone who can see the words and guess the password can unlock the message. Use a strong password and treat the word list like a ciphertext.
tools.base64.help.what: Converts text to Base64 and back. Useful when you need to shove binary-ish data through systems that only like plain text.
tools.base64.help.safe: Everything stays in your browser. Base64 is encoding, not encryption - it does not hide secrets.
tools.base64.help.watchOut: Don't treat Base64 as protection. Anyone can decode it instantly.
tools.bcrypt.help.what: Creates a one-way bcrypt hash of a password, and can check whether a password matches an existing hash.
tools.bcrypt.help.safe: Hashing and verification run locally. Nothing is uploaded. Bcrypt is designed to be slow on purpose, which makes guessing harder.
tools.bcrypt.help.watchOut: Bcrypt is for passwords you want to check later - not for encrypting files you need to recover. You cannot reverse a hash back into the password.
tools.hmac.help.what: Builds an HMAC-SHA256 signature for a message using a shared secret, so you can prove the data wasn't changed.
tools.hmac.help.safe: Signing happens in your browser. The secret key and message stay on your device.
tools.hmac.help.watchOut: HMAC only helps if the secret stays secret. If someone else has the same key, they can forge signatures too.
tools.jwt.help.what: Splits a JWT into header and payload so you can read the claims. Useful for debugging auth tokens.
tools.jwt.help.safe: Decoding is local - the token never leaves your browser. This tool does not fully validate signatures against a trusted server key.
tools.jwt.help.watchOut: A decoded JWT is still sensitive. Don't paste production tokens into random websites; here at least it stays on your machine.
tools.pgpKeys.help.what: Generates an OpenPGP key pair in the browser for encrypting and signing email or files.
tools.pgpKeys.help.safe: Key generation is client-side. Private keys are not uploaded.
tools.pgpKeys.help.watchOut: Your private key is long-lived identity. Protect it with a strong passphrase and never share it. Losing it can lock you out of old messages.
tools.photoCipher.help.what: Hides an encrypted message inside a photo in a way that usually survives JPEG recompression on Discord, Instagram, or similar apps.
tools.photoCipher.help.safe: Embedding and extraction run locally with AES-256. Without the password, the hidden data should look like ordinary image noise.
tools.photoCipher.help.watchOut: Very aggressive re-encoding or cropping can still damage the payload. Keep a backup of the original encoded image.
tools.rsa.help.what: Creates an RSA public/private key pair for asymmetric encryption and signatures.
tools.rsa.help.safe: Keys are generated in your browser and never sent to a server.
tools.rsa.help.watchOut: Anyone with the private key can impersonate you or decrypt messages meant for you. Store it offline and encrypted.
tools.spectralCipher.help.what: Hides an image inside an audio file's spectrogram - the picture shows up when you look at the frequencies. Optional AES encryption.
tools.spectralCipher.help.safe: Encoding and decoding happen locally. If you set a password, the payload is encrypted before it is woven into the audio.
tools.spectralCipher.help.watchOut: Heavy audio compression or format conversion can blur the spectrogram. Prefer lossless or high-bitrate exports when sharing.
tools.sshKeys.help.what: Generates OpenSSH-compatible RSA key pairs for Git, servers, and shells.
tools.sshKeys.help.safe: Generation is local. Your private key never leaves the browser session unless you copy it somewhere.
tools.sshKeys.help.watchOut: Never share the private key. Anyone who has it can log in as you. Rotate keys if a machine is compromised.
tools.steganography.help.what: Hides an AES-encrypted message in the least significant bits of an image so the picture still looks normal.
tools.steganography.help.safe: Encryption and embedding run in your browser. Without the password, extracting meaningful data should fail.
tools.steganography.help.watchOut: Classic LSB stego breaks if the image is resized or heavily recompressed. Send the file as-is when you can.
tools.timeCapsule.help.what: Encrypts a message so it can only be unlocked after a future time, using public randomness from the drand network.
tools.timeCapsule.help.safe: The message is encrypted in your browser. The site may proxy drand for timing, but it never needs your plaintext.
tools.timeCapsule.help.watchOut: Once the unlock time arrives, anyone with the ciphertext can decrypt it. Don't rely on secrecy after the unlock moment.
tools.token.help.what: Generates high-entropy random tokens for API keys, session IDs, CSRF secrets, and similar.
tools.token.help.safe: Uses the browser's cryptographically secure random generator (Web Crypto). Generation stays on your device.
tools.token.help.watchOut: A token is only as safe as where you store it afterward. Don't commit secrets to git or paste them into chat logs.
tools.uuidUlid.help.what: Generates UUID v4 identifiers and sortable ULIDs for databases, APIs, and distributed systems.
tools.uuidUlid.help.safe: IDs are created locally with secure randomness. Nothing is sent anywhere.
tools.uuidUlid.help.watchOut: UUIDs/ULIDs identify records - they do not authenticate or encrypt anything by themselves.
chat.help.what: Without a password, a random secret is stored in the link fragment. Share the full link privately; the room name alone cannot open the chat.
chat.help.messages: Every chat message (and typing indicator) is encrypted in your browser with AES-GCM before it touches the realtime relay. The relay only sees ciphertext plus minimal room metadata (room id, presence count, message ids/timestamps). Servers do not keep message history.
chat.help.calls: Call setup (offers, answers, ICE) is encrypted the same way as chat. Live audio/video uses WebRTC with TURN-only relay so peer IPs stay hidden. Media is protected by WebRTC’s built-in DTLS-SRTP between participants - the TURN server forwards encrypted packets, not clear speech or video.
chat.help.files: Files are AES-GCM encrypted in your browser first. Preferred upload is first-party storage (upload.encrypt.click). If that fails, ciphertext is sent only to encrypt.click’s own API, which then relays it server-side to backup hosts - your browser never talks to those third parties directly. The download link and filename travel inside an encrypted chat message.
chat.help.safe: Plaintext text, call media content, and file bytes are meant to stay client-side or end-to-end encrypted. Relays and upload hosts should only ever handle ciphertext for those payloads.
chat.help.watchOut: Without a password, a random secret is stored in the link fragment. Share the full link privately; the room name alone cannot open the chat.
security.chat.title: Encrypted chat, calls, whiteboard, and files
security.chat.p1: Chat messages, typing indicators, and call signaling are encrypted in the browser (AES-GCM) before they reach the relay. The relay forwards ciphertext and does not store chat message history.
security.chat.p2: Live calls use WebRTC with a TURN-only ICE policy so peer IP addresses are not exchanged directly. Media is protected by DTLS-SRTP between participants; TURN only relays encrypted packets. TURN credentials are fetched from encrypt.click (/api/turn).
security.chat.p3: Chat file attachments are encrypted client-side before upload, using the same ciphertext-first approach as Encrypt & share (first-party storage when available, otherwise server-side relay of ciphertext only).
security.chat.p4: Without a password, a random secret is stored in the link fragment. Share the full link privately; the room name alone cannot open the chat.
home.tools.title: All tools
home.tools.subtitle: Everything runs in your browser. No account, nothing to install.
security.share.title: Encrypted message and file sharing
security.share.p1: Encrypt & share runs AES-GCM in your browser before anything is uploaded. The password stays on your device unless you copy or send it yourself.
security.share.p2: Automatic upload prefers first-party ciphertext storage (upload.encrypt.click). That path is limited (about 50 MB) and availability is guaranteed for about 24 hours. If it fails, your browser posts ciphertext only to encrypt.click's upload API, which may relay server-side to temporary Send-compatible hosts. Those hosts should see ciphertext and server egress - not a direct browser upload of plaintext.
security.share.p3: Recipients open links on encrypt.click (often /u). Encrypted material may sit in the URL fragment (not sent to our servers on normal page loads) or point at uploaded ciphertext. Optional PNG wrapping can hide the share link in an image for offline handoff.
security.chat.p5: Whiteboard sessions use the same realtime infrastructure for collaborative strokes and state. Treat room access like chat: use a strong password for anything sensitive.
security.network.li5: The deployment check compares freshly fetched assets and the build manifest from this server. It cannot prove the authenticity of the code running in your browser or protect against a compromised host.
